title: Security Groups & Network ACLs 🛡️
description: Two layers of firewall: stateful instance protection and stateless subnet filtering.

slides.title: Two Firewalls, Two Jobs 🔥
slides.content:
# Security Group vs Network ACL

- **Security Groups (SG)**: operate at the **instance** level (actually at the Elastic Network Interface). They are **stateful** – if inbound is allowed, outbound response is automatically allowed.
- **Network ACLs (NACL)**: operate at the **subnet** level. They are **stateless** – both inbound and outbound rules must be explicitly defined.

Both are free, but they serve different purposes in a defense‑in‑depth strategy.

quizData.question: Which firewall type automatically allows return traffic when an inbound request is permitted?
quizData.explanation: Security Groups are stateful; return traffic is allowed even without an explicit outbound rule. NACLs are stateless and require both directions to be defined.

slides.title: Security Groups: Revisited & Refined 🔐
slides.content:
# Deep Dive on Instance‑Level Protection

- Default SG: all inbound denied, all outbound allowed.
- Custom SG: you add **allow rules only** (no deny rules).
- You can reference other security groups as sources (e.g., allow web servers SG to talk to database SG).
- Multiple SGs can be attached to an instance; rules are aggregated.

**Rule of thumb**: Use SGs to control traffic between application tiers.

slides.title: Network ACLs: The Subnet Gatekeeper 🚧
slides.content:
# Stateless Filtering

- Default NACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic.
- Custom NACL starts by denying everything; you add rules.
- Rules are **numbered** and evaluated in order (lowest number first).
- NACLs support both **allow** and **deny** rules.
- Because they are stateless, you must explicitly allow ephemeral ports for return traffic (e.g., TCP 1024‑65535).

**Use case**: Block a specific IP from an entire subnet (e.g., an attacker IP).

slides.title: NACL Rule Evaluation Order 📜
slides.content:
# Numbers Matter

Rules are evaluated starting from the lowest number. Once a rule matches, the action (allow or deny) is taken, and no further rules are evaluated.

- Use 100‑increment numbering (100, 200, 300) so you can insert rules later.
- The last rule is always an implicit deny (`*` rule).

Example: Rule 100 allow HTTP from 10.0.0.0/16; Rule 200 deny HTTP from 10.0.1.5/32. A request from 10.0.1.5 hits rule 100 first and is allowed unless rule 200 is renumbered before 100.

slides.title: Pro Tip: Defense in Depth 🏰
slides.content:
## Use Both Together

A robust security posture uses **both** SGs and NACLs:
- NACLs act as a broad subnet‑level barrier (e.g., block malicious IPs).
- SGs provide granular, stateful control per instance.

Don't rely on only one layer.
